claims.text: Ethanol-oxidation performance of nanoscale PGM catalysts is governed by formation of a dynamically stabilized submonolayer surface oxide.
Potential cycling under reaction conditions induces the proposed submonolayer oxide.
The submonolayer oxide modulates the catalyst's d-band electronic structure.
Modulation of the d-band optimizes adsorption energies of ethanol and its reaction intermediates.
Optimized adsorption energies enhance ethanol-oxidation activity, selectivity, and durability.
The initial nanoscale PGM catalyst has a clean, predominantly metallic surface.
Controlled potential cycling or pretreatment promotes formation of a submonolayer oxide on the PGM surface.
At approximately 0.5–1.0 V versus RHE, partial oxidation of the PGM can occur without full oxide formation.
The proposed submonolayer oxide is stabilized by strain.
Intrinsic nanoscale strain and the catalyst's surface structure facilitate formation of the submonolayer oxide.
A shift in the d-band center adjusts adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation reactants and intermediates.
The oxide-induced electronic modification promotes multi-electron and proton-transfer steps in ethanol oxidation.
The submonolayer oxide mitigates catalyst poisoning and dissolution.
Mitigation of poisoning and dissolution produces greater activity, improved product selectivity, and longer durability.
Potential-pretreated catalysts will have higher ethanol-oxidation turnover frequencies than untreated catalysts.
Potential-pretreated catalysts will produce fewer undesired byproducts than untreated catalysts.
Potential-pretreated catalysts will be more durable under operating conditions than untreated catalysts.
The beneficial effect occurs only in a moderate potential window that sustains the submonolayer oxide.
Performance improvements diminish or vanish when no oxide forms or when the catalyst surface becomes fully oxidized.
